plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure is one graph on a dotted coordinate grid showing two straight lines and the point at which they cross. The horizontal axis is labeled x and carries integer ticks from -6 to 6; the vertical axis is labeled y with integer ticks from -5 to 5, and each axis ends in arrowheads. A blue line of negative slope enters at the upper left and descends to the lower right, meeting the vertical axis just below the origin; a blue label at the left edge reads x + 2y = -1. A red line of positive slope climbs from the lower left to the upper right and meets the vertical axis at 3; a red label at the lower left reads -x + y = 3. Both lines end in arrowheads at each extremity. A filled black dot marks the single crossing, in the second quadrant just left of the vertical axis and slightly above the horizontal axis, and the coordinates printed above it read (-7/3, 2/3) with the fractions stacked. Drawing both equations against shared axes converts the algebraic system into a picture whose solution is a location. The graph makes visible that these lines meet at exactly one point, so the system has a single solution.

interactionPlan.concept: A system of two linear equations is solved by the single point that lies on both lines; changing a constant slides a line and changing a slope rotates it, which moves that crossing point or, when the slopes match, makes the lines parallel so no solution exists.
elements: x-axis with arrowheads and integer ticks from -6 to 6, labeled x
y-axis with arrowheads and integer ticks from -5 to 5, labeled y
light dotted background grid aligned to integer ticks
blue line of slope -1/2 (x + 2y = -1) with arrowheads at both ends
blue equation label 'x + 2y = -1' at the left edge
red line of slope 1 (-x + y = 3) with arrowheads at both ends
red equation label '-x + y = 3' at the lower-left edge
filled black intersection dot in the second quadrant
stacked-fraction coordinate label '(-7/3, 2/3)' printed above the dot
substitution readout panel (shown on click) displaying each equation with the dot's coordinates plugged in and both evaluating true

interactions.label: Blue line constant c in x + 2y = c
interactions.teaches: Sliding c translates the blue line vertically, and the black intersection point glides along the red line in response — the solution is whatever point currently lies on both lines, not a fixed location

interactions.label: Red line slope m in y = m x + 3
interactions.teaches: Rotating the red line about its fixed y-intercept (0,3) changes where it meets the blue line; when m reaches the blue slope (-0.5) the lines become parallel and the intersection vanishes, so the system has no solution

Selecting the black dot substitutes its coordinates into both equations and shows both statements come out true — the same ordered pair satisfies each equation, which is exactly what 'solution of the system' means

demo_steps.title: Two lines, one crossing
demo_steps.narration: The blue line x + 2y = -1 and the red line -x + y = 3 are drawn on shared axes; they cross at exactly one point, (-7/3, 2/3), so the system has a single solution.

demo_steps.title: Slide one equation
demo_steps.narration: Drag the blue-line constant c: the blue line shifts up or down and the black dot slides along the red line, showing the solution tracks the point that satisfies both equations at once.

demo_steps.title: Rotate into parallel
demo_steps.narration: Now lower the red-line slope toward -0.5 to match the blue line's slope: the lines turn parallel, the intersection leaves the plane, and the system switches from one solution to none.

demo_steps.title: Verify by substitution
demo_steps.narration: Restore the original lines and click the black dot: both equations light up with (-7/3, 2/3) substituted, each evaluating true — confirming the crossing point is the shared solution.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The solution of a linear system is the geometric intersection of its lines, so any change to a coefficient or constant moves that point — and equal slopes collapse it to no solution at all.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a faint dotted square grid on white. Draw the blue line with negative slope passing through (0,-0.5) and the red line with slope 1 through (0,3), each with arrowheads at both ends and a same-colored equation label near the left margin (blue upper-left, red lower-left). Mark the crossing with a solid black dot and a stacked-fraction label '(-7/3, 2/3)' just above it. On click, fade in a small readout panel (top-right) that prints 'x + 2y = -1 -> (-7/3) + 2(2/3) = -1  true' and '-x + y = 3 -> -(-7/3) + (2/3) = 3  true' with green check styling. When redSlope equals -0.5, hide the dot and fraction label and optionally show a 'parallel — no solution' note. Keep axis ticks and arrowheads exactly as in the source so the figure reads as the original textbook graph.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for the blue line's y-intercept: the learner shifts x + 2y = c up or down, the intersection point with the red line moves or exits the grid, and a system's solution is seen as the point satisfying both equations.
- Slider for the red line's slope: the learner rotates -x + y = 3 about its y-intercept, the crossing location updates and can become parallel to the blue line, clarifying how line orientation controls whether there is one or no visible solution.
- Click on the intersection point: the learner selects the black dot, both equations highlight and substitute the dot's coordinates, showing that the same ordered pair makes both equations true.

authoredContext:
We gain an important perspective on systems of equations by looking at the graphical representation. See the figure to find that the equations intersect at the solution. We do not need to ask whether there may be a second solution because observing the graph confirms that the system has exactly one solution.

This graph displays a system of two linear equations plotted on a coordinate plane. The blue line represents the equation x + 2y = -1, while the red line represents the equation -x + y = 3. The point where these two lines intersect, indicated by a black dot, is the solution to the system of equations and is labeled as (-7/3, 2/3). The x-axis ranges from -6 to 6, and the y-axis ranges from -5 to 5, with a grid background to aid in reading the coordinates.
